title: Segmented GPU pools: rate-limiting, eviction controls, and tenant-level throughput SLAs
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Background: As Dedicated customers scale, contention inside GPU clusters from mixed-tenancy workloads causes unpredictable tail latency and capacity exhaustion during bursts. Objective: introduce a segmented GPU pool model that enforces tenant separation via lightweight slice allocation, per-tenant throughput tokens, and deterministic eviction policies. Goals are: 1) provide throughput guarantees for reserved tenants, 2) limit noisy neighbor impact on best-effort tenants, 3) keep autoscaler behavior predictable when segments hit pressure.
proposal_summary: Create 'segments' (logical pool partitions) mapped to physical GPU pools. Each segment has: reserved_capacity (minimum gpus), burst_lane (short-lived soft-burst tokens), throughput_tokens (per-second token bucket for active requests per tenant), and eviction_profile (soft/hard eviction thresholds with tenant scoring). Admission controller will consult tenant QoS profile and current tokens before scheduling. Autoscaler will operate per-segment with cooldowns and cross-segment fallback rules. Public fallback allows best-effort requests to spill into a shared pool only if all reserved segments are saturated and policy permits.
acceptance_criteria: 1) A tenant with reserved_capacity=4 maintains >=90% of configured throughput under 2x normal load for 10 minutes without impact to p95 latency.
2) Noisy neighbor isolation reduces cross-tenant p95 latency increase to <10% when a best-effort tenant creates a synthetic 3x token storm.
3) Autoscaler respects per-segment min/max and scales within defined cooldown window; test automation verifies scale-up and scale-down sequences.
4) Eviction metrics (eviction_count, preempted_workloads) and token consumption appear on Console dashboards; alert fires when eviction_rate > 5/min for 3m.
5) Config-driven rollout (tenant opt-in) works; demo tenant toggles between segmented and legacy allocation without changing API keys.
design_decisions_and_tradeoffs: Decision: Logical segmentation vs strict hardware partitioning. We choose logical segmentation (scheduler-level) to maximize utilization and avoid overprovisioning at fleet scale. Tradeoff: slightly more complex eviction logic and potential cross-tenant syscalls; benefit: better bin-packing and lower $/token.

Decision: Soft eviction with scoring (age, priority, progress) rather than immediate hard preemption to avoid user-visible request truncation. Tradeoff: requires per-request progress signals and transient throttling but preserves graceful degradation.

Decision: Token-bucket throughput control at request admission rather than token per-token generated, to minimize runtime overhead. Tradeoff: coarse-grain control on large streaming requests — mitigated by a streaming token hook that deducts at chunk boundaries.
config_examples: burst_lane: 16  # short-lived tokens allowing temporary oversubscribe
api_changes: New admin APIs: POST /segments (create/update segment), GET /segments/{id}/metrics
New tenant APIs (admin-facing): PATCH /tenants/{id}/qos to set reserved_capacity and burst policy
Scheduler config: new config block 'segments' in fleet-config.yaml, supported by CLI 'rwctl segments apply'
Console: per-segment dashboards and 'simulate noisy neighbor' button for testing in staging
scheduler_changes: Admission controller checks tenant throughput_tokens and QoS before binding; rejects or queues requests when tokens are exhausted.
Soft-eviction flow: when segment saturation > threshold, compute eviction score across running jobs and throttle/evict lowest-scored jobs incrementally.
Spillover rules: if reserved segment is saturated and tenant permits, requests may be queued to public_shared segment based on priority and token availability.
Autoscaler coupling: segment-level metrics (util, queue_depth, burst_token_rate) are inputs to the autoscaler; autoscaler respects segment.min and segment.max values.
monitoring_and_alerting: New metrics: segment_utilization_ratio, tenant_throughput_tokens_used, eviction_count, preemption_latency_impact
Dashboards: dedicated > Segments Overview; single-tennant view showing reserved vs used GPUs and burst burn-rate
Alerts: segment_sustained_saturation (5m) -> paging when affected tenant impact=high; eviction_spike (eviction_count > 5/min for 3m) -> on-call alert
SLOs: p95 latency SLO per tenant tier; continuous bake tests will feed results into quality monitor
rollout_plan: 1) Internal milestone: implement segment metadata and scheduler admission - feature flag off (gas)
2) Staging: enable for non-critical system tenants; run synthetic noisy-neighbor scenarios for 72h
3) Canary: opt-in pilot with 2 customers on dedicated-1 (low-risk), collect metrics and support logs for 2 weeks
4) Gradual opt-in: open tenant QoS controls in Console; monitor eviction rates and autoscale churn; rollback plan ready
5) GA: enable by default for new Dedicated clusters; migration tooling to move existing reserved tenants into segments
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Token misconfiguration could starve best-effort workloads. Mitigation: safe defaults, audit dials in Console, and a 'grace' buffer in public_shared pool.
Risk: Eviction could cause wasted compute and client-visible errors. Mitigation: prefer throttling and graceful drain; emit detailed preemption reasons and provide client retry guidance in SDKs.
Risk: Autoscaler thrash across segments under oscillating load. Mitigation: per-segment cooldowns, hysteresis on scale-down, and aggregated view to prevent cross-segment ping-pong.
testing_plan: Unit tests for token-bucket admission and eviction scorer
Integration: simulate 50 tenants with mixed tiers, run 24h soak to validate utilization and eviction metrics
Chaos: introduce GPU node removals while segments under burst to validate eviction and fallback behavior
Performance: benchmark p50/p95 latency for reserved vs best-effort with and without burst enabled
End-to-end: staged customer pilot and acceptance test runbook linked in Confluence
